title: The McCumber Cube
content:
he McCumber Cube changed how I view security because it forces a three-dimensional perspective. I used to think of security simply as keeping hackers out with firewalls and strong passwords. But seeing the matrix of data states intersecting with the CIA triad made me realize that a single countermeasure is just a band-aid. Securing a database at rest requires completely different mechanisms than securing the same data when it is actively being processed in RAM or moving across a network.
What really stood out to me, though, was the emphasis on people and policies. We spend so much time in IT learning about the technical controls, but the cube places human behavior and organizational rules on the same level. A state-of-the-art intrusion detection system means nothing if an employee hands over their credentials in a phishing email because they were never trained. Every time we ignore one face of this cube, we leave a blind spot that someone can exploit. The model serves as a constant reminder that security is a comprehensive system, not just a collection of software tools.

title: Foundations of Information Security
content:
The traditional approach to security often feels heavily skewed toward prevention. We build walls, set up access controls, and try our hardest to keep threats on the outside. But studying the functional controls—prevention, detection, and mitigation—shifted my mindset. I realized that assuming prevention will always work is a dangerous trap. Defenses will inevitably break down, whether through a zero-day exploit or a simple human error.
When that initial barrier falls, detection becomes our only lifeline. It is terrifying to think that without proper logging and sensor networks, an attacker could wander around a system for months without anyone noticing. I now see detection not just as a secondary measure, but as the core of incident response. Once a threat is found, mitigation is about controlling the blast radius. Pulling a server off the network or revoking compromised credentials immediately is what prevents a minor breach from turning into a headline-making disaster. Accepting that perfect security is impossible actually makes it easier to focus on finding the breach and stopping the bleeding quickly.

title: AAA Framework
content:
The AAA framework completely demystified how access should be managed. Initially, I lumped the concepts of logging in and having permissions into one vague idea. Separating them into authentication, authorization, and accounting provides a much clearer roadmap for designing secure systems. Authentication is the first hurdle, proving identity through something you know, have, or are. It is obvious now why passwords alone are no longer enough; single factors are too fragile, making multi-factor authentication a mandatory baseline.
But proving who you are is only the beginning. Authorization dictates exactly what that identity is allowed to do. I have seen how poorly configured authorization can lead to privilege escalation, where a basic user account suddenly gains access to sensitive databases. The most eye-opening part for me, however, was accounting. Keeping detailed logs of every action ensures non-repudiation. When an incident occurs, there is no guesswork or deniability. The logs tell the exact story of what an account did, which is essential not just for stopping an ongoing attack, but for understanding how it happened in the first place.

title: Key Security Principles
content:
Learning the core security principles fundamentally altered how I approach system design. Concepts like least privilege and need-to-know are grounded in a healthy dose of paranoia, operating on the assumption that any account could already be compromised. By restricting permissions to only what is immediately necessary and separating sensitive duties among multiple people, the potential damage of a single failure drops significantly. Defense in depth builds on this by layering controls, so if a primary defense like a firewall fails, a host-based system is there to catch the fallout.
I also developed a deep appreciation for how systems handle failure. Failing into a safe, locked state rather than defaulting to open prevents a crash from becoming a gateway for an attacker. Complete mediation ensures that trust is never assumed after an initial login; every single action must be verified. Perhaps the most counterintuitive lesson was open design. It is tempting to hide how a system works to protect it, but true security relies on robust, publicly tested mechanisms like open cryptography, rather than the fragile hope that an attacker just won't figure out the code. Keeping the design simple, following the economy of mechanism, reduces the surface area for hidden vulnerabilities to take root.

title: The Threat Landscape
content:
Studying the various categories of information security threats completely reshaped how I perceive digital risk. I previously viewed security breaches through a narrow lens, assuming they were mostly limited to a handful of familiar cyberattacks executed by generic hackers. Examining the landscape more closely revealed a far more intricate environment. Learning to distinguish between crackers, who break into systems with intent to harm, and phreakers, who specifically target telecommunications, clarified how specialized these attackers have become. The technical sophistication of polymorphic malware, which mutates its underlying code to bypass signature-based detection, demonstrated that adversaries are constantly refining their methods. Even non-human threats, like fires or floods, which I initially dismissed as mere physical accidents, proved to be severe risks to data availability and business continuity.
This complexity made me realize the absolute necessity of shifting from a reactive posture to a proactive mindset. Waiting for an incident to occur before responding is no longer a viable strategy, especially as attacks grow more advanced. Security requires continuous anticipation through threat hunting and rigorous penetration testing to minimize the attack surface before an exploit happens. I also recognized the importance of practical, hands-on defense mechanisms. Tools like Security Information and Event Management platforms, such as Splunk, and Intrusion Detection Systems like Suricata are essential for monitoring networks in real time. Coupled with strict digital hygiene to defend against social engineering, these proactive measures form the foundation of a resilient system. Looking ahead, especially with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, anticipating emerging risks early is the only way to maintain a secure environment.

title: Risk Assessment
content:
The material helped me see risk assessment as a way to connect what an organization values with the ways it could be harmed. Assets include information, software, and equipment, but the information on a device may matter more than the device itself. I also found it useful to distinguish a threat, which could cause harm, from a vulnerability, a weakness that could make the harm possible. Looking at both helps explain why a risk exists instead of naming only a possible attack. The customer database example made that relationship clearer: identifying a weakness in an interface gives context to the threat of information being obtained.
The CIA Triad helped me consider what the impact could mean: disclosure affects confidentiality, improper changes affect integrity, and lost access affects availability. The McCumber Cube also reminds me that safeguards should cover information in storage, processing, and transmission, with technology supported by policies and user awareness. I now understand that an organization must weigh these protections against its legitimate need to use information and its tolerance for risk. Before recommending a safeguard, I should be able to explain what asset it protects, which weakness it addresses, and what consequence it helps reduce. This is a useful starting point.

title: Information Security Audit
content:
The Capytech assessment helped me understand how an audit can describe both existing safeguards and areas that need attention. The department reported private repositories, separate development and production environments, role-based access, and automated backups. The findings also showed why each control needs to be checked where it is used: multifactor authentication was reported for repositories and cloud consoles, while email MFA was marked absent. I found the credential-sharing discussion useful too. Sending a password in a separate email can still leave it exposed if both messages are reachable through the same compromised mailbox. A recommendation should explain that limitation without claiming that a key was leaked when the report found no leaked key.
I learned to treat missing evidence carefully. An unanswered checklist item was undetermined, not proof that a control was absent, and the phishing account did not establish its exact technical cause or any client-data loss. Likewise, backups and a previous restoration suggest recovery capability, but further testing is needed to confirm coverage and performance. For a small team with cost constraints, priorities such as email protection, controlled credential sharing, and recurring employee preparation need clear owners and evidence of completion. In future assessments, I want to distinguish confirmed findings from open questions and recommend practical steps that can be verified. That keeps conclusions dependable.
